The space station, a relic of a forgotten era, hung in the silent void like a metallic seed pod. Its orbit around the desolate planet was not a graceful arc but a precarious tether, the station’s hull groaning under the gravitational tug of the barren world below. The planet itself was a study in abandonment; its surface was a tapestry of cracked obsidian and rust-colored dust, devoid of any sign of life or atmosphere, a ghostly sphere that had long since surrendered its heat to the cold expanse of the cosmos.

Inside, the station’s metallic corridors stretched into shadows, their surfaces scarred by micrometeoroid impacts and the slow creep of oxidation. The air was stale, recycled through filters that had not been changed in decades, carrying the faint, metallic tang of old machinery. The solitary hum of the life-support systems was the only sound, a low, rhythmic drone that seemed to vibrate in the bones of anyone who dared to walk its halls. It was a sound of persistence, a mechanical heartbeat refusing to cease in the face of absolute isolation.

Outside the reinforced viewing ports, the universe unfolded in stark contrast to the station’s claustrophobic interior. A ballet of asteroids drifted through the inky backdrop of space, their jagged forms catching the distant light of a dying star. They moved with a slow, deliberate grace, colliding and separating in a cosmic dance that had been playing out for eons. Each rock was a fragment of a larger whole, broken apart by some ancient cataclysm, now drifting aimlessly in the void. The scene was both beautiful and terrifying, a reminder of the chaotic forces that shaped the universe and the fragility of the tiny, fragile station that dared to exist within it. The station was a speck of order in a sea of chaos, a testament to human ingenuity and resilience, even as it slowly succumbed to the entropy of the cosmos.
